neh.name: Nehemiah
neh.title: Carrying the people back home
neh.frame: Someone in Scripture was living somewhere safe when news arrived about people and a place he deeply cared about.
neh.intro: Nehemiah served the king of Persia in the city of Susa, far from Jerusalem. He had a steady place there. Part of his heart was still with the people back home.
story: One day, men arrived from Judah. Nehemiah’s first question wasn’t about life in Susa. He asked about the people back home, and about Jerusalem.
The answer wasn’t reassuring. The people who had survived were in great trouble. Jerusalem’s wall was broken down, and its gates had been burned.
He was far away and safe, yet the news reached him deeply. He sat down and wept. For several days he mourned, fasted and prayed.
Nehemiah didn’t dismiss his grief because he was somewhere safer. He let the news matter. Then he brought what was happening far away to God.
neh.invite: Read slowly. Notice what he does when the news arrives.
neh.q: What feels familiar about Nehemiah’s story?
options: It’s not the place I miss most. It’s my family and friends.
It’s hard knowing that people I care about are struggling while I’m somewhere else.
What’s happening in my country stays with me, more than people around me realize.
Sometimes I don’t know what I can do from here.
neh.prayer: God, the people I love feel far away today, and so does the trouble they’re in. You see them even when I can’t. Please be near them, and near me here. I bring You what I can’t fix from this distance. Amen.
neh.reflect: Who back home are you carrying in your heart right now?

hagar.name: Hagar
hagar.title: The God who sees
hagar.frame: Someone in Scripture found herself alone in the wilderness after being hurt by the people around her.
hagar.intro: Hagar was an Egyptian servant in Abram and Sarai’s household, a woman living far from her own people.
story: After Hagar became pregnant through an arrangement made by Sarai and Abram, conflict grew in the household. Sarai treated her harshly, and Hagar ran away.
She ended up in the wilderness, by a spring of water, away from everyone she had known.
And there, someone found her. God spoke to her by name, and asked where she had come from and where she was going. She answered honestly.
The encounter doesn’t begin with Hagar finding God. God finds Hagar. He tells her He has heard her affliction.
hagar.invite: Read slowly. Notice what Hagar calls God.
hagar.q: What feels familiar about Hagar’s story?
options: Sometimes I wonder whether anyone really sees what I’m carrying.
I can be away from the people who know me best and feel alone.
I want to know that God sees what’s happening, even when I don’t know what happens next.
hagar.prayer: God who sees, I’m not always sure anyone notices what I’m carrying. You found Hagar where she was. Please find me here too, and let me know I am seen. Amen.
hagar.reflect: What would you want God to see about today?

ps142.name: David
ps142.title: A prayer from the cave
ps142.frame: Someone in Scripture knew what it was like to look around and feel that no one was there.
ps142.intro: Before David became king, there were years when he was running for his life. Psalm 142 remembers him hiding in a cave.
story: David wasn’t speaking from a place of victory. He was hidden away and afraid, with no one beside him.
He told God plainly what it was like: no one was concerned for him, and no one cared for his life.
Then something significant happens. David doesn’t correct himself or say he shouldn’t feel this way. He pours out his complaint first.
Only afterwards does he tell God that He is his refuge.
ps142.invite: Read slowly. You can read verse 4 twice.
options: He tells God plainly that he feels alone.
He doesn’t hide his complaint from God.
He feels like no one notices what he’s carrying.
Even when no one seems to see him, he believes God knows his way.
ps142.prayer: God, sometimes I look around and no one seems to be there. I pour out what I’m carrying to You, just as it is. Be my refuge today. Amen.
ps142.reflect: If you told God plainly what today is like, what would you say?

ruth.name: Ruth
ruth.title: Stepping into the unknown
ruth.frame: Someone in Scripture stepped into a new life without knowing what it would become.
ruth.intro: Ruth was a young widow from Moab. Her mother-in-law, Naomi, had lost her husband and both sons, and was going home to Bethlehem.
story: Naomi urged Ruth to stay behind among her own people and rebuild her life there.
Ruth chose to go anyway. She wasn’t moving because everything had worked out. She was leaving her country for another, her people for Naomi’s people, and a familiar future for an uncertain one.
Her choice was full of love. It also came in the middle of death, separation and leaving home. Something good and something painful were happening at the same time.
ruth.invite: Read slowly. Notice what Ruth holds on to.
ruth.q: What feels familiar about Ruth’s story?
options: I’m leaving something familiar behind.
I don’t know what my future here will look like, or where my studies will lead.
Something good and something painful are happening at the same time.
I’m trying to belong here, and to build a future too.
ruth.prayer: God, I’m standing between what I’ve left and what I don’t know yet. Some of it is good and some of it hurts. Walk with me into this next season, my studies, my work and my future, the way You walked with Ruth. Amen.
ruth.reflect: What are you hoping for in this new place, and what are you afraid of?

hannah.name: Hannah
hannah.title: A song after a long season
hannah.frame: Someone in Scripture brought a good thing to God after a long season of waiting.
hannah.intro: For years, Hannah longed for a child. Year after year she went with her family to worship, and year after year she came home with the same ache.
story: Someone close to her provoked her, and there were times she wept and couldn’t eat.
One year she poured out her heart to God so deeply that the priest watching misunderstood her. She told him she had been pouring out her soul before the LORD.
Later her son Samuel was born. When Hannah prayed again, it was a song.
Her song doesn’t pretend the hard years didn’t happen. It carries them, and still gives thanks.
hannah.invite: Read slowly. Notice who Hannah thanks.
hannah.q: What feels familiar about Hannah’s story?
options: Something good came after a long, hard season.
I want to thank God, and I remember what it took to get here.
The good is real, even if not everything is fixed.
I was misunderstood once. Today I can breathe a little.
hannah.prayer: God, thank You for the good thing in front of me. You know the long road it took to get here. Help me receive it without fear, and remember that it came from You. Amen.
hannah.reflect: What good thing would you like to thank God for today?

samaritan.name: the Samaritan
samaritan.title: Coming back to say thank you
samaritan.frame: Someone in Scripture had something good happen, and he was the only one from somewhere else.
samaritan.intro: Ten men with a skin disease called out to Jesus from a distance. Their illness kept them apart from others. One of them was a Samaritan, an outsider even among them.
story: Jesus told them to go and show themselves to the priests. On the way, all ten were healed.
Only one turned back. He came praising God in a loud voice and fell at Jesus’ feet to thank him. He was the Samaritan.
Jesus noticed. He asked where the others were, and then he spoke to the man who had come back, the one from somewhere else.
samaritan.invite: Read slowly. Notice who comes back, and who notices him.
samaritan.q: What feels familiar about this story?
options: Something good happened, and I want to tell someone.
I’m the one from somewhere else here.
I want to turn back and say thank you.
I was noticed when I didn’t expect to be.
samaritan.prayer: God, something good happened, and I want to bring it back to You. When I feel like the one from somewhere else, remind me that You notice me. Thank You. Amen.
samaritan.reflect: Who would you tell about this good thing, if they were close?

hab.name: Habakkuk
hab.title: How long?
hab.frame: Someone in Scripture looked at the harm around him and asked God how long it would go on.
hab.intro: Habakkuk was a prophet in Judah. Around him he saw violence, injustice and people being hurt, and it seemed that nothing was being done.
story: He didn’t keep quiet about it, and he didn’t take his complaint somewhere else. He took it straight to God.
His prayer begins with a question many people still ask. How long?
Habakkuk’s honest words were kept in Scripture. What stirred him up about the wrong he saw did not push him away from God. It brought him to God.
hab.invite: Read slowly. You don’t have to soften anything.
options: He asks God how long, without softening it.
He names the harm he sees instead of looking away.
He doesn’t understand, and he keeps talking to God anyway.
He wants God to act, and says so.
hab.prayer: God, I don’t understand why this happened. I bring it to You as it is. You see what is wrong more clearly than I do. Please act, and hold me while I wait. Amen.
hab.reflect: What would you want to say to God about what happened, if you didn’t have to be polite?

mary.name: Mary
mary.title: If you had been here
mary.frame: Someone in Scripture came to Jesus with a loss and a question she couldn’t hold back.
mary.intro: Mary and her sister Martha were close friends of Jesus. When their brother Lazarus became very ill, they sent word to him. By the time Jesus came, Lazarus had died.
story: Mary had been grieving for days, surrounded by people who came to mourn with the family.
When she saw Jesus, she fell at his feet and said what was in her heart. If he had been there, her brother would not have died.
Jesus didn’t correct her or tell her to stop crying. He saw her weeping, and he was deeply troubled. Then Jesus wept.
mary.invite: Read slowly. Notice what Jesus does before he says anything more.
mary.q: What feels familiar about Mary’s words?
options: “If you had been here…” I have questions like that too.
I’ve lost something that shouldn’t have been lost.
I want to know God is moved by what hurts me.
I can bring my honest words, not only polite ones.
mary.prayer: Jesus, I have questions I can’t answer, and a loss I didn’t want. You wept with Mary. Please stay with me in this too. Amen.
mary.reflect: Is there an “if only” you would like to bring to God?

joseph.name: Joseph
joseph.title: What was meant for harm
joseph.frame: Someone in Scripture found good in his life, and never pretended the wrong done to him was small.
joseph.intro: As a young man, Joseph was sold by his own brothers and taken to Egypt. For years he was a servant and then a prisoner, far from his family.
story: In time, God brought Joseph out of prison and into a place of great responsibility. When famine came, his brothers travelled to Egypt for food and found him there.
After their father died, the brothers were afraid Joseph would pay them back for what they had done.
Joseph wept. He did not call what they did small. He said plainly that they had meant it for harm. He also said that God had been at work, bringing good out of it.
joseph.invite: Read slowly. Notice that he names the harm and the good in the same breath.
options: He calls the wrong what it was.
Something good came, and the hurt was still real.
It took him many years to reach these words.
He sees God at work even in a painful story.
joseph.prayer: God, thank You for the good in my life right now. You also know what was done to me, and that it was wrong. I place both in Your hands, so I don’t have to carry the wrong alone. Amen.
joseph.reflect: What good would you like to hold on to, and what would you like to hand over to God?

elijah.name: Elijah
elijah.title: A still, small voice
elijah.frame: Someone in Scripture felt like the only one left, and was worn out from standing alone.
elijah.intro: Elijah was a prophet who stood up for God when very few others would. After a great struggle, his life was threatened, and he ran.
story: He went into the wilderness, exhausted. God’s first answer was not a lecture. An angel woke him, gave him bread and water, and let him sleep again.
Then Elijah walked to Mount Horeb and stayed in a cave. There he told God everything: how hard he had worked, what had been done, and that he felt like the only one left.
God passed by. There was a great wind, an earthquake and a fire, but God was not in them. After the fire came a still, small voice.
elijah.invite: Read slowly. Notice where God is, and where He isn’t.
options: He feels like he’s the only one left.
He tells God exactly how hard it has been.
God gave him food and rest before any words.
God came in a quiet voice, not in the storm.
elijah.prayer: God, I’m tired of carrying this alone, and stirred up by what has happened. Give me what I need today: rest, bread and Your quiet voice. Amen.
elijah.reflect: What would help you rest a little today?

ps77.name: Asaph
ps77.title: When words won’t come
ps77.frame: Someone in Scripture was too troubled to speak, and prayed anyway.
ps77.intro: Psalm 77 was written by Asaph, a worship leader. In a time of trouble he cried out to God by day and by night.
story: Asaph led worship among God’s people. Psalm 77 doesn’t say exactly what had gone wrong. It says that in the day of his trouble he reached out to God all night, and nothing comforted him.
He couldn’t sleep. He was so troubled he couldn’t find words. He even asked the hardest questions: had God forgotten to be kind? Would it always be like this?
Then he made a choice. He started to remember what God had done before, how He led His people through the sea when there seemed to be no way through.
The psalm doesn’t say his trouble ended that night. It shows someone bringing honest questions to God, while holding on to what God had already done.
ps77.invite: You don’t need to understand every line. Let the words speak for you.
options: He is too troubled to speak.
He keeps crying out, even at night.
He remembers God, even when it hurts.
I don’t have words either.
ps77.prayer: God, I don’t have the words right now. You already know. Please stay close. Amen.
ps77.reflect: If one word comes to mind, you can write it here.

ps13.name: David
ps13.title: When the waiting is long
ps13.frame: Someone in Scripture asked God “How long?” and kept praying.
ps13.intro: Psalm 13 is a short prayer David prayed when God felt far away. He asks “How long?” four times, then chooses to trust.
ps13.invite: You can ask God the same question. Honest complaint is a kind of prayer.
options: I’ve been waiting a long time.
It feels like God is far away.
I want to trust, even now.
ps13.prayer: God, how long will this last? Sometimes it feels like You are far away. I’m telling You honestly. Help me trust Your love, even now. Amen.
ps13.reflect: What would you ask God, if you could ask anything?

ps61.name: David
ps61.title: From the end of the earth
ps61.frame: Someone in Scripture called to God from far away when his heart was overwhelmed.
ps61.intro: In Psalm 61, David calls to God from far away, with his heart overwhelmed, and asks to be led somewhere steady.
ps61.invite: Read verse 2 slowly. You can call to God from wherever you are.
options: I feel very far from home.
My heart is overwhelmed.
I need somewhere steady to stand.
ps61.prayer: God, I am far from home and my heart is overwhelmed. Hear me from here. Lead me to the rock that is higher than I. Amen.
ps61.reflect: Where do you need God to be steady for you?

ps62.name: David
ps62.title: Pour out your heart
ps62.frame: Someone in Scripture invited God’s people to pour out everything before Him.
ps62.intro: Psalm 62 invites God’s people to trust Him at all times and to pour out their hearts to Him, all of it.
ps62.invite: You don’t have to tidy your words first.
options: There’s a lot inside me.
I don’t know where to start.
I need a safe place.
ps62.prayer: God, here is everything I’m carrying, poured out before You. You are my refuge. Amen.
ps62.reflect: What would you pour out first?

ps56.name: David
ps56.title: God keeps your tears
ps56.frame: Someone in Scripture, far from home and afraid, said God keeps every tear.
ps56.intro: David wrote Psalm 56 while far from home and afraid. He says God counts his wanderings and keeps every tear.
ps56.invite: None of your tears are lost to God.
options: I’ve moved around a lot.
I’ve cried more than people know.
I want to know God sees it.
ps56.prayer: God, You count my wanderings and You keep my tears. Thank You that nothing I carry is lost to You. Amen.
ps56.reflect: What would you want God to remember for you?

ps139.name: David
ps139.title: Known before you speak
ps139.frame: Someone in Scripture said God knew him completely, even his unspoken words.
ps139.intro: In Psalm 139, David says God knows him completely, even the words he hasn’t said yet.
ps139.invite: You don’t need to find the words. You are already known.
options: I can’t explain what I feel.
I want to be fully known.
I need to know God understands.
ps139.prayer: God, You know me completely. You know the words I can’t find. Thank You that I am known and loved by You. Amen.
ps139.reflect: If one word comes to mind, what is it?
